A California Apple user has filed a class-action lawsuit accusing Apple of misleading consumers about the privacy protections of its "Hide My Email" feature. Here are the details.

Apple Sued Over Alleged 'Hide My Email' Vulnerability

404 Media previously reported that Apple was aware of an alleged vulnerability over a year ago that could expose the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias.

Apple's "Hide My Email" feature lets users create unique, randomly generated email addresses that forward messages to their personal inbox, allowing them to sign up for apps, websites, and newsletters without revealing their real email address.

The feature is available for free through Sign in with Apple, while a more comprehensive version included with an iCloud+ plan (starting at $0.99 per month) lets users create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher alerted Apple in June 2025 to a vulnerability that could expose the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias.

Apple acknowledged receiving the report about a month later but allegedly never fixed the issue. In March 2026, the company said it had patched the vulnerability, but the researcher found it was still exploitable.

404 Media reported as follows:

Regarding the lawsuit (reported by MacRumors), plaintiff Anthony Alvarez stated:

Apple has known about the issue for over a year, yet the vulnerability remains unfixed—at the same time, Apple continues to profit from "Hide My Email" and its privacy promises. The plaintiff is one of millions of customers who paid for iCloud+ and trusted Apple's claim that "Hide My Email" would protect their personal email address. The plaintiff and class members paid Apple for privacy—iCloud+ subscribers through the premium portion of their iCloud+ subscription fees, and all Apple customers through the product premium associated with features like the so-called enhanced privacy protections and "Hide My Email" bundled into Apple products.

The lawsuit also claims this is not an isolated incident, citing a 2023 report that Apple's random MAC address feature could expose users' real hardware identifiers.

The complaint also alleges that the proposed class members' claims exceed $5 million in aggregate (excluding interest and costs), but does not explain how that figure was calculated.

Alvarez filed on behalf of himself and other Apple customers he claims were similarly affected. He is asking the court to certify the case as a class action covering four proposed user groups:

  • Nationwide Apple customers who purchased a device and used "Hide My Email";
  • A California subclass of the above users;
  • A nationwide subclass of iCloud+ subscribers who used the feature;
  • A California subclass of iCloud+ subscribers.

He is seeking a jury trial and, in addition to monetary damages in an amount to be determined, is asking the court to order Apple to fix the "Hide My Email" feature or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.

Do you think this class action should be certified? Let us know in the comments.
